content: The chikungunya virus is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected mosquito. Mosquitoes become carriers of the virus when they feed on a person who is already infected. Once infected, these mosquitoes can spread the virus to other individuals through subsequent bites. Symptoms of chikungunya typically appear 3 to 7 days after being bitten by an infected mosquito. The most common symptoms include fever and joint pain. Additional symptoms may include headache, muscle pain, joint swelling, or a rash. While most individuals recover within a week, some may experience persistent joint pain lasting for months. The mosquitoes responsible for spreading the chikungunya virus are found in many regions worldwide. Travelers visiting countries in Africa, Asia, the Americas, and islands in the Indian and Pacific Oceans are at risk of infection. These mosquitoes are active and bite during both the day and night. Currently, there are no vaccines or medications available to prevent chikungunya. Travelers can reduce their risk of infection by taking specific precautions. Using insect repellents registered with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) that contain active ingredients such as DEET, picaridin, IR3535, or oil of lemon eucalyptus (OLE) is recommended. These repellents are safe and effective when used as directed, even for pregnant and breastfeeding women. If sunscreen is also being used, insect repellent should be applied after sunscreen. For babies and children, additional precautions include dressing them in clothing that covers their arms and legs, covering strollers and baby carriers with mosquito netting, and carefully applying insect repellent. Products containing OLE or para-menthane-diol (PMD) should not be used on children under 3 years old. Insect repellent should not be applied to a child’s hands, eyes, mouth, cuts, or irritated skin. Adults should spray insect repellent onto their hands before applying it to a child’s face. If sunscreen is also used, apply the insect repellent after the sunscreen. Clothing and gear, such as boots, pants, socks, and tents, can be treated with 0.5% permethrin, an insecticide that kills or repels mosquitoes and other insects. Permethrin-treated clothing provides protection even after multiple washes. Always follow product instructions when treating items yourself, and do not apply permethrin directly to the skin. To keep mosquitoes out of your accommodations, choose lodging with air conditioning or window and door screens. If staying in a place without these features or sleeping outdoors, use a mosquito net. Mosquito nets should be compact, white, rectangular, and have 156 holes per square inch. Treated mosquito nets, especially those treated with permethrin, offer greater protection than untreated ones. Follow label instructions to determine if a treated net can be washed. If bitten by mosquitoes, avoid scratching the bites. Instead, apply over-the-counter anti-itch or antihistamine creams to relieve itching. For more information on mosquito bite symptoms and treatment, consult reliable medical resources.
